query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), brittle behavior emerges not from pre‐existing impurity segregation, but rather from stress‐induced short-range chemical ordering (SRO) localized at grain boundaries. Under mechanical loading (especially cyclic or at low temperatures), the deformation activates atomic rearrangements at the grain boundaries that foster local ordering. This transition reduces the cohesive energy of the boundaries, precipitating intergranular fracture—a mechanism that is distinct from the slow, thermally driven segregation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA with a disordered solid solution and uniformly high toughness.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled mechanical loading (e.g., cyclic or monotonic deformation up to a threshold strain) at service-relevant low temperatures, with a parallel set kept undeformed.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant loading conditions at temperatures where embrittlement is a risk (e.g., below ambient or in low-temperature environments) and under cyclic loading environments that simulate fatigue in service.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of localized short-range order (SRO) at grain boundaries induced by deformation.
generation.mechanism: The applied stress promotes atomic rearrangements at the grain boundaries. This in-situ evolution from a fully random chemical distribution to a locally ordered state reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries, triggering brittle intergranular fracture. Unlike conventional alloys where grain-boundary embrittlement stems from impurity segregation or secondary brittle precipitate formation, here the mechanism is dynamically induced by service loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-processed baseline, mechanically loaded specimens will show (i) a measurable increase in SRO at grain boundaries (detectable by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM), and (ii) a corresponding decrease in toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness or a shift in the fracture mode from ductile to intergranular brittle failure) under the same loading conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-processed HEA in which the grain boundaries are uniformly disordered, exhibiting high ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under loading conditions that are severe enough to trigger atomistic rearrangements (e.g., high cycle fatigue or high strain rate loading) and particularly at temperatures where the kinetics of ordering are activated. Its relevance may be limited if loading is insufficient or if the temperature is such that atomic mobility is too low for any significant ordering.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which stress-induced SRO develops at grain boundaries in HEAs under service conditions is not yet well documented, and distinguishing these changes from other deformation-related features could pose a challenge. Additionally, current spatial resolution limits could obscure early-stage SRO detection, leaving some uncertainty in the precise quantification of the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA samples. Subject one set to controlled mechanical loading (cyclic deformation at a relevant low temperature) while keeping the other set as an undeformed control. Conduct post-deformation characterization using high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to detect any changes in the chemical order at grain boundaries. Follow this with mechanical testing (fracture toughness tests and microscopic fractography) to evaluate the mode of failure.
measurements: Quantification of SRO at grain boundaries via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM.
Fracture toughness and tensile ductility measurements.
Microstructural analysis of fracture surfaces to ascertain intergranular vs. transgranular cracking.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically deformed samples do not exhibit any statistically significant increase in SRO at the grain boundaries relative to the control, or if the fracture mode remains ductile and similar to the baseline behavior despite deformation, then the hypothesis—that stress-induced SRO reduces grain-boundary cohesion and triggers brittle failure—should be rejected.
